title: Dynamic Programming
oneLiner: If you know exactly how the world works, you can compute the best strategy by repeatedly applying the Bellman equations until the numbers stop changing.

what.html:
Dynamic programming (DP) solves an MDP when you have its full rulebook (every probability and reward). It works by sweeping over all states again and again, each time improving every state's value using its neighbours' values. Two main recipes: value iteration (always take the best action in the update) and policy iteration (fully score a strategy, then improve it).

Everyday versionPlanning a road trip with a perfect map: start from the destination and work backwards, writing on each town how long it takes to get to the end from there. A few passes over the map and every town has its best route.

why.html:
• It gives the exact answer that every other RL method is trying to approximate.
  • The pattern "evaluate, then improve" is behind almost every RL algorithm.
  • It shows clearly what you lose when you don't have a model.

how.title: Score a fixed strategy
how.html: Policy evaluation: start all values at 0 and keep applying "value = expected reward + γ × expected next value" for the strategy until the numbers settle.

how.title: Always take the best action
how.html: Value iteration does the same sweep but uses the best action's value in each state. When values stop changing, read off the best action in each state.

how.title: The race car
how.html: A car is Cool or Warm. Driving fast pays +2 but can warm the engine; driving fast when Warm overheats it (−10, game over). Starting from 0, value iteration gives (2, 1), then (3.35, 2.35), and settles at Cool 15.5, Warm 14.5: fast when cool, slow when warm.

how.title: Use fresh numbers straight away
how.html: Updating values in place (using a state's new value immediately for the next state) spreads information faster: on the race car it needed about 20% fewer sweeps.

how.title: Policy iteration
how.html: Pick a strategy, work out its exact values, switch each state to the action that looks best under those values, and repeat. When nothing switches, it's optimal. The race car needs just two rounds.

how.title: Which one to use?
how.html: Policy iteration: few rounds, each expensive. Value iteration: many rounds, each cheap. Both get the same answer.

how.title: The big pattern
how.html: Generalised policy iteration: keep making the values match the strategy, and the strategy greedy for the values. They pull against each other until both are optimal. Nearly every RL method follows this pattern.

demo.html: Press Play to run value iteration on the race car two ways at once. The in-place version (green) reaches the optimum, Cool = 15.5, in fewer sweeps. Try a stricter stopping threshold.

example.html:
One improvement step. Under "always slow", the car earns 1 forever: value 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10 in both states. Now ask: from Cool, what if I go fast once and then follow "always slow"? 2 + 0.9 × 10 = 11, better than 10. So switch Cool to fast. From Warm, fast gives −10: keep slow. Re-scoring the new strategy gives 15.5 and 14.5, and nothing improves further.

Supplementary DP needs the model. The next sessions learn the same values from experience instead.

takeaways: DP solves known MDPs using Bellman equations as updates.
Value iteration: repeated max backups; race car → (15.5, 14.5).
Policy iteration: evaluate fully, improve greedily, repeat.
GPI (evaluate ⇄ improve) underlies almost all RL.
thirty: Dynamic programming computes values and optimal policies for an MDP with a known model. Iterative policy evaluation applies Bellman expectation backups until changes fall below θ. Value iteration applies optimality backups, V ← maxₐ Σp[r + γV], then extracts a greedy policy; on the race-car MDP (γ = 0.9) it goes (0,0) → (2,1) → (3.35, 2.35) → v* = (15.5, 14.5), with policy fast when Cool and slow when Warm. In-place (asynchronous) sweeps use fresh values and converge faster. Policy iteration alternates full evaluation with greedy improvement, justified by the policy improvement theorem; from (slow, slow), valued (10, 10), it reaches the optimum in two cycles. Generalised policy iteration, the interaction of evaluation and improvement, describes nearly all RL methods.
